column1: What does a scalar user-defined function return?
column2:
One value of a declared SQL data type.
For example, a tax function returns one decimal amount per evaluation. It does not return the rows that make up an order.
Review source

column1: What is the minimum number of input parameters for a scalar UDF?
column2:
Zero.
Declare an empty parameter list and still call the function with parentheses, as in dbo.GetCode(). The empty parentheses identify a function call.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCode ()
RETURNS int
AS
BEGIN
    RETURN 42;
END;
GO
SELECT dbo.GetCode();
Review source

column1: Where can you use a scalar UDF call that you cannot put an ordinary stored-procedure call?
column2:
A scalar UDF can be used inside a SQL expression.
Use a scalar UDF where a single value fits, such as a column expression in SELECT. Fabric Warehouse restricts scalar UDF use in queries on user tables to eligible inlined calls.
SELECT dbo.DoubleNumber(10) AS Result;
-- Result: 20
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column1: Which clause declares a scalar UDF's return data type?
column2:
RETURNS.
RETURNS specifies the type SQL Server uses for the result. A tax function declared as DECIMAL(10,2) returns a value with two fractional digits.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.DoubleNumber (@number int)
RETURNS int
AS
BEGIN
    RETURN @number * 2;
END;
Review source

column1: What does RETURN send to the caller of a scalar UDF instead of a procedure's integer status code?
column2:
The UDF returns its calculated value, not an integer execution-status code.
RETURN gives the UDF caller the value declared by RETURNS. In an ordinary procedure, RETURN instead exits with an integer status code.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.DoubleNumber (@number int)
RETURNS int
AS
BEGIN
    RETURN @number * 2;
END;
Review source

column1: Why put a shared calculation in a scalar UDF?
column2:
To keep one reusable implementation of the calculation.
For example, every invoice query can use the same tax calculation. Update the function when the formula changes rather than tracking down copies in separate queries.
Review source

column1: What makes a function deterministic?
column2:
It returns the same result for the same inputs and database state.
The function must produce the same result when neither its inputs nor the relevant database state changes. A system clock can change even when both stay fixed.
Review source

column1: Why does a tenure UDF that calls GETDATE() fail the determinism requirement for an indexed view?
column2:
GETDATE() makes the function nondeterministic.
Two calls with the same hire date can get different answers because the clock moves. Indexed view expressions cannot depend on that changing value.
Review source

column1: How can a tenure UDF use a repeatable reference date instead of reading the system clock?
column2:
Accept an explicit as-of date instead of calling GETDATE().
Pass the date you want the calculation to use. The calculation no longer depends on when it runs, but SQL Server also requires schema binding to mark the UDF deterministic.
Review source

column1: What restriction applies if a T-SQL scalar UDF tries to update a permanent application table?
column2:
UDFs cannot directly modify permanent database state.
The UDF can compute a value for an UPDATE statement, but it cannot perform the application-table update from its own body. Put the write in a procedure when needed.
Review source

column1: Why can a query caller not assume a scalar UDF runs once per row in a particular order?
column2:
Query optimization can change how the function is evaluated.
The optimizer can move, combine, or inline function logic. Treat the function as a calculation rather than a way to control the order of work.
Review source

column1: Why can a non-inlined scalar UDF be costly on a large result set?
column2:
Repeated function calls can add overhead for every qualifying row.
When many rows need the result, separate invocations add overhead. Without inlining, the optimizer cannot optimize the function's statements together with the whole calling query.
Review source

column1: Which SQL Server 2019-and-later feature can remove separate calls to eligible T-SQL scalar UDFs?
column2:
Scalar UDF inlining.
Inlining can substitute the function's logic into the calling plan as expressions or subqueries. SQL Server must consider both the definition and the call eligible.
Review source

column1: Which function form exposes reusable tabular query logic as a single SELECT statement?
column2:
An inline table-valued function.
An inline TVF returns rows from one SELECT. Because the result is tabular, replace a scalar call with a table source such as FROM or APPLY when rewriting the caller.
Review source

column1: Why can DATEDIFF(YEAR, @HireDate, @AsOfDate) overstate tenure before the hire-date anniversary?
column2:
It counts year boundaries, not completed anniversaries.
December 31 to January 1 crosses one calendar-year boundary even though only one day passes. Completed tenure must account for whether the hire anniversary occurred.
SELECT DATEDIFF(YEAR, '20241231', '20250101');
-- Result: 1
Review source

column1: A scalar UDF accepts a phone number as VARCHAR(10). Why can its body miss extra ASCII characters?
column2:
The value can be truncated before the function body sees it.
SQL Server converts the input to VARCHAR(10) before the body runs. A length check inside the function cannot recover the missing characters.
Review source

column1: Which statement changes an existing scalar UDF without dropping its permissions?
column2:
ALTER FUNCTION.
ALTER FUNCTION updates the existing object and keeps its granted permissions. Callers still need compatible parameter and result types.
ALTER FUNCTION dbo.DoubleNumber (@number int)
RETURNS int
AS
BEGIN
    RETURN @number * 2;
END;
Review source

column1: What error does DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS avoid?
column2:
The missing-function error when the named function does not exist.
IF EXISTS skips the drop when the function is absent. It does not allow an unauthorized drop or remove a schema-bound dependency.
DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS dbo.DoubleNumber;
Review source

column1: Which catalog view helps inspect recorded SQL dependencies before dropping a function?
column2:
sys.sql_expression_dependencies.
Query this view for recorded expressions that reference the function. It is not a complete list of calls built dynamically or made from application code.
Review source

column1: What kind of dependency can prevent SQL Server from dropping a scalar UDF even with IF EXISTS?
column2:
A schema-bound function or view that references the function.
Schema binding protects the referenced definition. Address the dependent object before removing the function, even if the drop uses IF EXISTS.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, how must you qualify a scalar UDF name when calling it in a SELECT expression?
column2:
At least schema.function_name, such as dbo.CalculateSalesTax.
Write the schema and function name followed by an argument list. A function without arguments still needs parentheses.
SELECT dbo.DoubleNumber(10) AS Result;
-- Result: 20
Review source
